entries.seminar_title: The Supply of Expertise: New Technologies, New Skills, and Worker Impacts
entries.speaker: Cäcilia Vom Baur
entries.abstract: Does educational content respond to technological advances, and do such changes enable workers to acquire new valuable expertise? We construct a novel database of legally binding training curricula spanning the near universe of vocational training in Germany over five decades, and link curriculum updates to breakthrough technologies using Natural Language Processing. We trace a causal chain from technological change to curriculum content to worker outcomes. Technological change spurs curriculum updates, and training content shifts toward less routine-intensive tasks. This shift occurs predominantly through the emergence of new skills related to social, digital, and problem-solving competencies, rather than the removal of old ones. This within-occupation margin is quantitatively important: curriculum updates account for two-thirds of the overall deroutinization in vocational skill supply over this period. Using administrative employer-employee data and a stacked difference-in-differences design, we show that new-skilled workers earn higher wages, especially in technology-exposed occupations, and are more likely to remain employed in their trained occupation. In contrast, older occupational incumbents experience wage declines, indicating skill obsolescence.

entries.seminar_title: Simple Standard Errors for Complicated (Quasi-)Experimental Designs
entries.speaker: Jonathan Roth
entries.abstract: We develop standard errors for estimates of causal effects in settings where the distribution of treatment exposures is known but potentially exhibits complicated dependence patterns across units. Such dependence arises, for example, in settings with spillovers/interference across units or when the treatment assignment is spatially correlated. Our variance estimator generalizes several properties of the Neyman variance estimator for completely randomized experiments to general designs: it is unbiased for an upper bound on the variance from the design-based perspective; the conservativeness of this upper bound depends on the heterogeneity of treatment effects; and it is also valid under certain forms of super-population sampling of the potential outcomes. Our estimator reduces to standard approaches in simple designs, such as the Neyman variance estimator in completely randomized experiments and the cluster-robust variance estimator in cluster-randomized experiments. We show that the proposed estimator is admissible among the class of quadratic-form variance estimators, and derive asymptotic conditions under which it is consistent for an upper bound on the asymptotic variance of the treatment effect estimator. In simulations and applications based on two empirical studies, one with peer effects and another with a spatially correlated treatment, we find that the proposed variance estimator performs well, and in some cases yields standard errors that are 2-3 times shorter than those of existing alternatives.
